title: Hidden Angular Momentum Loop Currents in Symmetric Crystals
authors: Rule Yi, Vincent P. Flynn, Benedetta Flebus
abstract: Loop-current order has been invoked to explain unconventional electronic phases, with the crystal lattice usually regarded as a passive host for the underlying collective dynamics. Here we show that circulating currents can originate in the lattice itself, sustained by quantum and thermal fluctuations. We develop a microscopic description of angular momentum exchange that separates transfer between sites from crystalline restoring torques and reveals how circulation can emerge in a symmetry-preserving equilibrium state. In a two-dimensional elastic lattice preserving time-reversal, inversion, and fourfold rotational symmetries, we uncover opposite current loops on neighboring plaquettes while the mean angular momentum vanishes at every site. These currents are sustained by zero-point fluctuations in the phonon vacuum and persist at finite temperature. We trace their origin to directional elastic interactions in locally symmetry-lowered environments, with the higher crystal symmetry organizing the resulting currents into a compensated pattern of circulation. Our results extend the physics of equilibrium loop currents to lattice dynamics, revealing that elastic geometry can organize fluctuations into persistent angular momentum circulation without electronic or magnetic order, external driving, or spontaneous symmetry breaking.
summary: This work shows that crystal lattice vibrations (phonons) can generate persistent, circulating angular momentum currents even in highly symmetric materials where the average angular momentum is zero. This phenomenon arises from directional anisotropies in the elastic interactions, demonstrating that lattice geometry itself can organize fluctuations into a measurable, non-trivial quantum state.
main_problem: To demonstrate that persistent, circulating angular momentum currents can exist within the crystal lattice itself, sustained by quantum and thermal fluctuations, even when the average angular momentum at every site is zero.
main_result: Opposite, compensating current loops can form around neighboring plaquettes due to directional elastic interactions, establishing a mechanism for equilibrium angular momentum circulation without electronic order or external driving.
method: The authors develop a microscopic description of angular momentum exchange, analyzing the lattice Hamiltonian using phonon dynamics and considering the separation of site-to-site transfer from restoring torques.
model_or_system: The study focuses on a minimal two-dimensional elastic lattice preserving high symmetries (time-reversal, inversion, fourfold rotation), applicable to materials like cuprates. The physics is governed by the lattice's elastic response tensor and local bonding environments.
key_observables: Phonon angular momentum current ($\langle \hat{J}_{A 	o B} angle$), mean angular momentum at each site (zero), and cross-polarization correlations.
important_parameters: Zero-point fluctuations (quantum) and finite temperature (thermal); directional elastic stiffnesses ($\Gamma$ vs $\Gamma^T$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on harmonic equilibrium approximations and the existence of local anisotropy in bonding environments, even if the global structure is highly symmetric.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the mechanism using schematic diagrams of angular momentum exchange in isolated pairs and show the effective A–B lattice structure derived from parent elastic networks.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by first establishing the microscopic description of angular momentum exchange, then applying it to a 2D elastic lattice model, deriving the current's dependence on local anisotropies, and finally providing symmetry arguments to constrain the current's expectation value.
why_interesting: The concept of emergent, non-zero circulation from zero mean values due to fluctuating geometry is highly relevant to understanding exotic quantum phases in condensed matter, bridging lattice dynamics with topological concepts.
